summary.one_liner: Colorama makes ANSI escape sequences for colored terminal text and cursor positioning work on Windows, and does nothing on other platforms.
summary.what_it_does: Wraps stdout/stderr and converts recognised ANSI color and cursor sequences into win32 console calls, so Python output using ANSI codes displays correctly on Windows. The newer just_fix_windows_console() function (since v0.4.6) enables Windows' built-in ANSI support on recent Windows 10+ consoles, or wraps the streams on older versions. The older init() function adds keyword options: autoreset, strip, convert, and wrap. It also provides Fore, Back and Style constants for basic colors and styles, plus deinit()/reinit() to turn it on and off. Only a defined subset of ANSI sequences is converted (basic 8 colors, bright/dim/normal, cursor movement, and screen/line clearing); other sequences are stripped on Windows. On non-Windows platforms it does nothing by default.
use_cases: Show colored terminal output from Python scripts on Windows
Make existing ANSI-colored CLI output work on Windows
Print colored text with Termcolor or Rich on Windows
Reset terminal colors automatically after each print
Strip ANSI codes when output is redirected to a file
Position the cursor in a terminal UI on Windows
notable: Calling just_fix_windows_console() is a no-op on non-Windows platforms
Works alongside libraries like Termcolor, Blessings, and Rich rather than generating new ANSI codes itself
Limited conversion: only a documented subset of ANSI sequences is handled
Dim text looks the same as normal text on Windows
caveats: Only a limited subset of ANSI sequences is recognised; others are silently stripped on Windows
On Windows, Colorama does not support ANSI dim text; it looks the same as normal text
The init() interface can cause side-effects and must not be called multiple times; it is recommended to use just_fix_windows_console() instead
